title: Rise of Communism under Stalin in Russia (1917–1939)
tagline: The struggle for succession, the Five Year Plans, collectivisation and the purges between 1917 and 1939.

overview.intro: The Soviet Union between 1917 and 1939 was transformed from a war-damaged agrarian empire into an industrial state by policies imposed from the centre at extraordinary human cost. This unit traces the establishment of communism after the October Revolution, the struggle between Trotsky and Stalin for the succession to Lenin, the forced industrialisation of the Five Year Plans, the collectivisation of agriculture and the famine that followed, and the great purges through which the party and society were brought under control.

facts.label: Consolidation
facts.value: Bolshevik power secured through the civil war of 1918–20, the Red Army, War Communism and the Cheka.

facts.label: Succession
facts.value: Lenin died in 1924; Stalin, as general secretary, outmanoeuvred Trotsky, Zinoviev and Kamenev and emerged supreme by 1929.

facts.label: Plans
facts.value: First Five Year Plan from 1928, the second from 1933; heavy industry prioritised over consumer goods.

facts.label: Purges
facts.value: The great purges of 1936–38 with mass arrests, show trials and executions; the purges extended to the army.

learningOutcomes: Describe how communist rule was established and consolidated in Russia.
Explain the struggle for succession after Lenin’s death.
Assess the aims and results of the Five Year Plans.
Evaluate the great purges and their effect on Soviet society.

blocks.text: The Bolsheviks who took power in October 1917 held the cities and the centres of communication but faced opposition on every side. The civil war of 1918–20 pitted the Red Army against a loose coalition of White forces supported by foreign intervention, and the Bolsheviks prevailed through superior unity, control of the railways and the central industrial region, and the concession of the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk that took Russia out of the war. Internally the party governed through War Communism, which nationalised industry and requisitioned grain, and through the Cheka, which suppressed opposition. The cost was famine in 1921 and the Kronstadt revolt of the same year, after which Lenin replaced War Communism with the New Economic Policy, which permitted small-scale private trade and replaced grain requisitioning with a tax in kind.

The structure of rule was built alongside the economy. Power was concentrated in the party, which admitted members on the basis of discipline and controlled the soviets at every level, while the party’s own apparatus was organised through a growing secretariat. Lenin’s Testament, written in 1922 and 1923 as his health failed, warned against the accumulation of power in that secretariat and made critical comments about Stalin’s rudeness, but it was not publicly presented in full, and its effect was blunted by the rivalries of those it mentioned.

items: The Treaty of Brest-Litovsk removed Russia from the war at a heavy territorial cost.
The civil war was won on unity, communications and the industrial centre.
War Communism requisitioned grain and nationalised industry, producing famine and revolt.
The New Economic Policy of 1921 restored a limited market economy.
The party apparatus, not the soviets, became the true instrument of power.

blocks.text: Lenin died in January 1924 and no single figure inherited his authority. Trotsky was the most obvious successor, as the organiser of the Red Army and the most gifted orator, but he held no party post of consequence and repeatedly misjudged the importance of the party machine. Stalin, appointed general secretary in 1922, used that post to place his supporters throughout the party in a series of appointments, so that by the time of a vote the delegates owed their positions to him. He allied first with Zinoviev and Kamenev against Trotsky, whom he expelled in 1927, then isolated Zinoviev and Kamenev by combining with Bukharin against them, and finally removed Bukharin from influence once his own position was secure.

blocks.caption: How Stalin outmanoeuvred his rivals
rows: Isolated Trotsky from the party apparatus

blocks.text: Behind the manoeuvring lay a real dispute about policy. Trotsky and the left argued for rapid industrialisation financed by the peasantry; the right, led by Bukharin, favoured a slower pace with the New Economic Policy continued. Stalin’s position shifted to whichever side was useful, and once he adopted forced industrialisation in 1928 he had no further need of the right. By 1929 he was unchallenged, and the following decade of Soviet policy carried the mark of that victory.

learn.title: The Five Year Plans and collectivisation

blocks.text: The first Five Year Plan began in 1928 with the objective of transforming the Soviet Union from a peasant country into an industrial power capable of defending itself. Priority went to heavy industry: coal, steel, electricity, machinery and armaments, with new industrial cities such as Magnitogorsk built from scratch with the assistance of foreign engineers. The plan was pushed through at extraordinary speed, and while the statistical targets were often met on paper through inflated reporting, the physical results were substantial, with coal and steel output multiplying and a new industrial base created in the Urals and Siberia.

The agricultural side was collectivisation, which from 1929 sought to replace individual peasant holdings with large state and collective farms so that the state could control the food supply and finance industrialisation through grain exports. Peasants responded by slaughtering their livestock rather than surrendering it, and the country lost a very large share of its cattle and pigs within two years. The denial of grain, particularly in Ukraine, the Kuban and Kazakhstan, where the state imposed impossible procurement targets and confiscated seed grain, produced the famine of 1932–33 in which millions died. The policy secured state control over grain and released labour to the cities, but at the cost of a permanent hostility between the countryside and the regime and a reduction in agricultural output that took years to recover.

Financing of industry through grain exports
Elimination of the prosperous peasant as a class

blocks.text: The purges began with the trial of the so-called Trotskyites in August 1936, in which old Bolsheviks confessed to sabotage and conspiracy, and continued through a second trial in 1937 and the military trial of 1938. Confessions were produced by interrogation, psychological pressure and promises, and the defendants were executed after public trial. The purges reached the party, the state administration, the intelligentsia and finally the armed forces, where a large proportion of senior officers was removed, tried and executed in 1937–38, which left the Soviet military badly weakened on the eve of war.

The mechanisms extended beyond Moscow. Quotas were issued to the regional security organs for arrests and executions, a process formalised by NKVD order 00447 in 1937, and national minorities such as Poles, Germans and Koreans were deported. The Gulag system of labour camps expanded to provide forced labour for construction projects in extreme conditions. Society was reorganised through terror in which any failure could be reported as sabotage, so that denunciation became a means of personal advancement or self-protection.

Historians continue to debate the purpose and the scale. Some older interpretations emphasised a bureaucratic state purging itself, and later work using the archives has emphasised that the violence was driven from the top and used to resolve problems the regime had created, including the hostility produced by collectivisation. What is not in doubt is the outcome: opposition was destroyed as an organised force, the party and the state apparatus were rebuilt around personal loyalty to Stalin, and the repression left a legacy that affected Soviet politics and society for decades.

items: Show trials of 1936–38 presented confessions from former party leaders.
The army lost a large share of its senior officers before the war.
Regional arrest and execution quotas were issued by the NKVD.
National minorities were deported and the camp system expanded.
Denunciation became a means of survival within the system.

questions.prompt: The policy introduced in 1921 to replace War Communism was:
questions.explanation: The NEP permitted small-scale private trade and replaced requisitioning with a tax in kind after famine and revolt.

questions.prompt: Stalin’s principal advantage in the succession struggle was:
options: His control of the party secretariat and appointments
His command of the Red Army
questions.answer: His control of the party secretariat and appointments
questions.explanation: As general secretary he could appoint and promote officials, so party votes were shaped before they were cast.

questions.prompt: The collectivisation of agriculture led directly to:
options: Slaughter of livestock and the famine of 1932–33
questions.answer: Slaughter of livestock and the famine of 1932–33
questions.explanation: Peasants killed livestock rather than surrender it, and the confiscation of grain in Ukraine and elsewhere caused famine.

questions.prompt: The purges of 1937–38 weakened the Soviet Union before the war chiefly because:
options: A large proportion of senior army officers was removed and executed
questions.answer: A large proportion of senior army officers was removed and executed
questions.explanation: The destruction of experienced senior commanders left the armed forces poorly led at the moment of the German invasion.

questions.prompt: The struggle for leadership after the death of Lenin in 1924 was between Trotsky and Stalin, among __________ .
questions.explanation: Zinoviev, Kamenev and Bukharin were also eliminated in successive stages.

questions.prompt: The system of forced-labour camps that expanded under Stalin is known as the __________ .
questions.explanation: The camps provided forced labour for construction projects in extreme conditions.

questions.prompt: State four measures adopted under the Five Year Plans.
questions.answer: Four measures are: priority for heavy industry such as coal, steel, electricity and machinery; rapid construction of new industrial centres and cities such as Magnitogorsk, using foreign engineers; the collectivisation of agriculture so that the state controlled the food supply; and the direction of labour, with workers subject to discipline and movement restricted by internal passports. Urbanisation of the workforce is also accepted.
questions.explanation: Each measure should be linked to the aim of rapid industrialisation and defence capacity.

questions.prompt: Explain how Stalin secured the leadership of the party between 1924 and 1929.
questions.answer: Lenin left no settled successor, and Stalin’s advantage was his post as general secretary, from which he could make and confirm the appointments on which party officials depended. He first worked with Zinoviev and Kamenev to isolate Trotsky, who was expelled from the party in 1927 and later exiled. He then turned against his former allies, defeating Zinoviev and Kamenev with the support of Bukharin and the right, who favoured a slower pace of industrialisation within the New Economic Policy. Having used them, he moved against the right in 1928–29, removing Bukharin from the Politburo once he had adopted the policy of forced industrialisation himself. By manipulating the party apparatus, shifting his alliances and controlling the ideological line at each stage, he emerged by 1929 as the unchallenged leader.
questions.explanation: The answer must show the sequence of alliances and the mechanism of control, not merely name the rivals.

questions.prompt: Assess the results of the Five Year Plans in the Soviet Union.
questions.answer: The plans sought to transform a peasant country into an industrial power, and in this objective they succeeded substantially within a decade. Coal, steel and electricity output multiplied, a heavy industrial base was created in the Urals and Siberia, cities such as Magnitogorsk were built, and the country acquired the capacity to produce armaments on a scale that would prove decisive in the Second World War. Urbanisation proceeded rapidly and the workforce was trained in industrial discipline. The costs were severe. Finance came from controlling agriculture and exporting grain, which required collectivisation, and collectivisation provoked the slaughter of livestock and the famine of 1932–33 in which millions died. Consumer goods were consistently subordinated to heavy industry, so living standards improved slowly. The plans also depended on forced labour, on statistics that were inflated for reporting purposes, and on an apparatus of terror that reached its height in the purges. The assessment therefore has to hold both halves together: as a project of industrial transformation the plans achieved a great deal in very little time, and as a policy they were purchased with famine, coercion and a permanent breach between the regime and the countryside.
questions.explanation: Full marks require concrete achievement and concrete cost in the same answer, ending with a reasoned judgement.

questions.prompt: Were the great purges of 1936–1938 an expression of Stalin’s strength or of his insecurity? Answer with evidence.
questions.answer: The case for strength is that only a leader in undisputed control could order the arrest, trial and execution of former party leaders, senior generals and regional officials on such a scale, and that the trials demonstrated publicly that no individual and no past service placed anyone beyond reach. The quotas issued to regional organs and the public confessions suggest a state machinery fully responsive to central direction, and the result was a party and state apparatus rebuilt around personal loyalty. The case for insecurity rests on the same evidence read differently: a leader with secure support does not need confessions from old Bolsheviks to justify removing them, and the very scale of the arrests, extending through the army and the minorities, indicates that perceived opposition was imagined to be everywhere. The purge of the senior officer corps in 1937–38 is particularly telling, since it removed experienced commanders on the eve of war and could not have been justified by their disloyalty, and the fact that the violence began after the trauma of collectivisation suggests that the regime was suppressing the resentment its own policies had produced. The most defensible judgement is that the two are not opposites: the purges expressed a strength that was real, since no one could resist the centre, and a insecurity that was equally real, since the policies of the previous decade had created constituencies of grievance which terror alone could hold in check. Both readings are supported by the same institutional evidence, and the answer should show why.
questions.explanation: Full marks need both readings argued from the same concrete evidence and a judgement that explains why the evidence supports both.
